title: Animal Patterns Art
strapline: Spots, stripes and scales painted onto strips — and the real reason animals wear them.
intent: Children explore how animals' coats and skins help them survive in their habitat.
Copying and continuing a pattern is early mathematics in an art activity.
Close looking at a zebra or a leopard builds genuine observational skill.
Camouflage is a real, satisfying scientific idea that three- and four-year-olds can grasp.
Painting and collaging strips gives a manageable, repeatable surface to work on.
implementation: Provide clear pictures of zebras, giraffes, leopards, snakes and fish to look at closely.
Offer paint, printing tools and collage materials so children can choose their method.
Cut paper into strips so the task is contained and a child can finish one and start another.
Introduce the pattern vocabulary as they work: spots, stripes, scales, patches, rows.
Talk about camouflage — why a stripey animal is hard to see in long grass.
Support cutting and painting without doing it for them.
Display the finished strips together so the patterns can be compared.
key_questions: What pattern can you see on this animal?
What comes next in your pattern?
Why do you think a leopard has spots and a zebra has stripes?
Where would this animal be hard to see?
Can you make a pattern that nobody else has made?

impact.text: Children copy, continue and create simple patterns and talk about them.
Children develop observation skills and awareness of camouflage.
Children make choices about colour, material and tool and mix to see what happens.
Children talk about their own work and notice detail in others'.
Children use brushes and printing tools with intent and control.
Children take up new pattern and animal vocabulary and use it in play.

enhancements: A camouflage hunt — hide the finished strips around the room and try to spot them.
A pattern table with beads, pegs and blocks to continue the maths away from paint.
Animal masks made from the finished patterned strips.
A magnifier station with real feathers, shells and fur samples to look closely at.
A photograph challenge — find a pattern somewhere in the nursery.
A collaborative animal mural built from every child's strip.

playing_exploring: Children choose their animal, their pattern and their materials.
Printing and painting invite experimentation with what each tool does.
active_learning: Children repeat a pattern carefully across a whole strip.
They return to make several, refining as they go.
creating_thinking: Children work out the rule of a pattern and continue it.
They reason about why an animal might need to be hard to see.
